Below is a synthesis of how Niklas Luhmann’s systems theory describes cinema, grounded in his general theory of communication, differentiation, and autopoiesis, and in applications to art, media, and film.

Core concepts Luhmann brings to cinema
- Communication as structuration. In Luhmann’s view, society is composed of communication processes, not individuals acting on a common world; communication is a recursive “synthesis of three selections” (utterance, information, understanding) and occurs between communications, with psychic systems providing observation, expectation, and memory that feed and are fed by social systems. <cite id="e4b81f40-0">Communication is a three-fold selection: selection of utterance, selection of information, selection of understanding, and media arise as macro-structures to pre-select and streamline communication</cite> <cite id="e4b81f40-0">Observation, expectation and remembering are key; communications exist in time and must be tried again, so society builds “media” to facilitate remembering and pre-selection</cite> <cite id="e4b81f40-1">Communication processes are symbolically generalized couplings; Luhmann’s late work emphasizes observation and meta-observation as foundational, with media as symbolically generalized communication media</cite> <cite id="e4b81f40-3">Media of dissemination (writing, printing, broadcasting) remove time-space restrictions; language, dissemination media, and symbolically generalized communication media widen possibilities and connect psychic and social systems</cite>.
- Functional differentiation and subsystems. Modern society differentiates into autopoietic subsystems (e.g., politics, economy, science, art, law, religion, sport, health, education, mass media) whose operations are closed to each other and organized around binary distinctions; cinema belongs to the symbolic-media arts subsystems that select, store, and communicate cultural meaning. <cite id="e4b81f40-0">Ten systems can be enumerated and are autopoietic, operationally closed, with specific binary codes</cite> <cite id="e4b81f40-3">Language, dissemination media, and symbolically generalized media regulate communication possibilities and connect psychic and social systems</cite> <cite id="e4b81f40-2">Modern society observes itself through sciences and mass media; films, novels, and art participate in society’s self-observation</cite>.
- Autopoiesis and cultural production. Autopoietic systems reproduce themselves by producing and processing their own distinctions; in culture/arts, this means works and meanings are co-constituted in communicative couplings that are both self-referential and historically produced. <cite id="e4b81f40-2">Observation is one of the operations permitting systems to conduct self-referential and autopoietic reproductions; films and novels are legitimate parts of significant self-observations of society</cite> <cite id="e4b81f40-4">Luhmann’s approach identifies dominant characteristics of systems via symbolically generalized media; subsystems are “black boxes” with binary-coded communications</cite>.

Cinema as a communication system and medium of self-observation
- Cinema within mass media and culture. Luhmann treats mass media (news, advertisements, entertainments) as functional systems that communicate pre-selected differences to society; films are communicative artifacts produced within the arts system and circulate as media that present symbolized realities to society. <cite id="e4b81f40-0">Grand structures and “media” continuously arise to facilitate effective communication and remembering, pre-selecting and streamlining communication in society</cite> <cite id="e4b81f40-2">Modern society observes itself through mass media; what we know about our society we know through the mass media, which include films and entertainments</cite> <cite id="e4b81f40-3">Dissemination media expand reach across time and space; examples include writing, printing, and electronic broadcasting</cite>.
- Self-observation and reflexivity. Cinema participates in society’s “self-observation”: audiences learn themselves, their risks, norms, and conflicts through films, which means cinema is not only a cultural product but also a meta-communication that reflects and conditions social perception. <cite id="e4b81f40-2">Modern society’s essential task consists of self-observation via science and mass media; films are a legitimate part of this self-observation</cite> <cite id="e4b81f40-2">In particular, films of child abduction are considered self-observation of a risk society; the child becomes an indicator of a specific semantics constituted by the risk society</cite> <cite id="e4b81f40-0">Media are built up by communications within a system and are not “seen” by the systems using them; they provide pre-sets and configurations (language, values, structures) for effective communication</cite>.

Production and reception as couplings between observer/integration and observation
- Selection, storage, and distribution. Film production and exhibition operate as couplings that select, encode, and store differences (narratives, images, motifs) that can later be re-communicated; dissemination media (cinemas, broadcasting) make observation and expectation scalable across time and space. <cite id="e4b81f40-0">Media pre-select to streamline communication and remembering, making possible effective communication across time</cite> <cite id="e4b81f40-3">Dissemination media remove time-space restrictions and increase reach; they are built on language and broaden communication possibilities</cite>.
- Audiences as observers. Reception is not “meaning-making” by subjects but system-level selection: viewers distinguish utterance and information, align with selected codes, and thereby participate in reproducing the filmic system and its meanings. <cite id="e4b81f40-0">Understanding is the ability to differentiate between information and utterance; communication is a synthesis of three selections, independent of psychic understanding</cite> <cite id="e4b81f40-1">Observation is a technical notion as designation by distinction; systems (including psychic systems) observe themselves; the abstract notion of observation becomes central in Luhmann’s late work</cite> <cite id="e4b81f40-2">Accordingly, society knows itself through the mass media; films and art participate in this self-observation</cite>.

Autonomy, aesthetic paradox, and ambiguity in cinematic communication
- Art as a system of “fitting–not-fitting.” The arts system evaluates communicative artifacts by a functional paradox: works must simultaneously satisfy and violate criteria to count as art, a structure emphasized by Luhmann and critiqued as underdeveloped in theoretical terms. <cite id="34163fc7-1">Luhmann’s theory may frame cultural communication, but he provides limited theoretical development of the creative process in relation to culture and treats the arts as communication about art rather than through art</cite> <cite id="34163fc7-2">In Luhmann’s view, artworks communicate in a functional system driven by the paradoxical binary “fitting–not-fitting,” but this mode needs further theoretical development</cite>.
- Ambiguity and limits. Scholars note a tension between Luhmann’s binary coding and the ambiguous, open-ended character of aesthetic communication; cinema often relies on interpretive slippage that Luhmann’s strict dichotomies undertheorize. <cite id="34163fc7-1">Luhmann’s description of creation of the artwork mentions a “special kind of communication” but is not theoretically developed in relation to culture, and he describes the social system of the arts as communication about art rather than through art</cite> <cite id="34163fc7-2">Luhmann’s world is not very “physical” or “immediate,” and the paper theorizes “ambiguous communication” as central, contrasting with Luhmann’s binary “ambiguous–not-ambiguous” framing</cite> <cite id="34163fc7-2">Luhmann speaks of a “doubling” of meaning in mass media (constructing and making constructions realities) framed by “new information–old information,” creating a tension with a theory of “selection of ambiguity”</cite>.
- Media as “medium of media.” Cinema’s self-referential character is highlighted by its status in the mass media system as a medium that both explores possible realities and stabilizes them; filmic worlds exemplify the media’s role in constructing and validating social realities. <cite id="34163fc7-2">Mass-media construct reality or explore possible realities, e.g., in stories or sitcoms; “realities can be constructed and constructions can become realities”</cite> <cite id="e4b81f40-0">Media are built up over time by communications, invisible to the systems using them, and provide pre-sets and configurations for enduring and effective communications</cite>.

Cinema’s relation to other media and to society
- Coupling and differentiation. Cinema couples observer/integration systems (psychic systems) with observation systems (sensory, memory) via symbolically generalized media, extending language and dissemination technologies; it differs from language (symbolic generalization) and from broadcasting (distribution) in its integrated communicative form. <cite id="e4b81f40-3">Language, dissemination media, and symbolically generalized media operate as distinct layers; dissemination media expand reach, while language widens possibilities and connects psychic and social systems</cite>.
- Cultural communication and mass media. Within cultural communication, cinema is a specialized subsystem that communicates cultural pre-sets (values, norms, expectations) while also being evaluated by the arts system’s paradoxical criteria. <cite id="34163fc7-1">Cinema fits within cultural communication but Luhmann’s account undertheorizes the “special kind of communication” of art</cite> <cite id="34163fc7-2">The arts system is driven by “fitting–not-fitting,” while mass media construct and stabilize realities through stories, creating a tension that needs reflection</cite>.
- Societal totality and risk/society. Film genres and cycles can be read as society’s self-observation of specific problematics (e.g., risk) and as indicators of collective semantics and concerns. <cite id="e4b81f40-2">Films of child abduction are considered self-observation of a risk society; the child in those films indicates a semantics of child shaped by risk society</cite>.

Processual and developmental accounts
- Autopoietic production and reproduction. Films are produced as communicative structures that select and store differences, then reproduced in reception and distribution; over time, media pre-sets and cultural codes shift, altering what counts as meaningful filmic communication. <cite id="e4b81f40-0">Media are built up by communications within a system and remain “invisible” to the systems using them; they provide pre-sets that enable enduring and effective communication</cite> <cite id="e4b81f40-0">Communication must be “tried again,” so structures and media continuously arise to facilitate remembering and pre-selection</cite>.
- Historical differentiation and self-referentiality. Cinema emerges within modern society’s differentiation as a subsystem that both reflects and conditions social observation; as a “medium of media,” it recursively models and modulates how society sees itself. <cite id="e4b81f40-2">Sociology and mass media are principal systems of society’s self-observation; films, novels, and art participate in this self-observation</cite> <cite id="e4b81f40-3">Symbolically generalized media and dissemination media regulate communication across time and space, enabling modern media systems</cite>.

Critical perspectives and limits
- Ambiguity, embodiment, and immediacy. Luhmann’s framework has been criticized for undertheorizing ambiguity, emotions, and physical immediacy in art and communication, which are vital to cinematic experience and reception. <cite id="34163fc7-1">Luhmann leaves gaps with culture-as-process, and his account of creation of artworks is not theoretically developed; he emphasizes communication about art over communication through art</cite> <cite id="34163fc7-2">Luhmann’s world is “not very physical” or “immediate,” leaving little room for play, performativity, and cultural communication that requires embodiment and immediacy</cite>.
- Idealism vs. materiality and specificity. Critics argue Luhmann treats systems as “black boxes” and risks idealizing communication over material structures and media technologies, which hampers detailed analysis of filmic production and reception. <cite id="34163fc7-1">Luhmann’s description of the arts system as communication about art rather than through art is seen as insufficient</cite> <cite id="34163fc7-2">Luhmann’s “doubling” of meaning is framed by “new information–old information,” creating a tension with ambiguity</cite> <cite id="34163fc7-4">Luhmann’s approach identifies dominant characteristics via generalized media but offers little specificity; systems often remain mythical “black boxes” with possible arbitrariness in media-coding</cite> <cite id="34163fc7-4">Luhmann’s interpretation of communication media can seem idealistic with little room for the material world</cite>.

Putting it together: a Luhmannian description of cinema
- As a system: Cinema is an autopoietic subsystem of modern society that produces and reproduces its own distinctions through communicative artifacts; it is organized around binary codes (e.g., inside/outside, sense/reference, fitting/not-fitting) and is operationally closed from other subsystems. <cite id="e4b81f40-0">Systems are operationally closed and autopoietic; media arise to pre-select and streamline communication</cite> <cite id="34163fc7-2">Artworks communicate in a functional system driven by “fitting–not-fitting”</cite>.
- As communication: Film production and exhibition operate as couplings that select, encode, and distribute information; audiences receive as observers, differentiating utterance and information and thereby sustaining the filmic system. <cite id="e4b81f40-0">Communication is a three-fold selection; media pre-select to facilitate remembering and communication</cite> <cite id="e4b81f40-1">Observation is designation by distinction; late Luhmann centers observation and meta-observation</cite>.
- As self-observation: Cinema mediates society’s self-reflection—genres and cycles can be read as expressions and regulators of collective concerns (e.g., risk)—making film both mirror and mold social perception. <cite id="e4b81f40-2">Society knows itself through the mass media; films participate in this self-observation</cite> <cite id="e4b81f40-2">Films of child abduction exemplify self-observation of a risk society and index a risk-related semantics</cite>.
- As a medium of media: Cinema exemplifies the media’s power to construct and stabilize realities; narrative worlds and images become shared realities that can then be re-communicated across time and space. <cite id="34163fc7-2">Mass media construct and make constructions realities, e.g., through stories</cite> <cite id="e4b81f40-3">Dissemination media remove time-space constraints and expand reach, enabling modern communication systems</cite>.
- As art: Its aesthetic status depends on a paradoxical coupling—simultaneous adequacy and inadequacy to criteria—reflecting the arts system’s evaluative mode, even as Luhmann’s formalization struggles with ambiguity and embodiment. <cite id="34163fc7-2">Art communication is driven by the “fitting–not-fitting” paradox</cite> <cite id="34163fc7-1">Luhmann’s account is criticized for undertheorizing ambiguity and for focusing on communication about art rather than through art</cite>.

Practical implications for studying film
- Analyze film as communicative selection: focus on how scripts, editing, and sound select “differences” (events, rhythms, gaps) that are communicatively bound to audience codes. <cite id="e4b81f40-0">Communication requires the three selections (utterance, information, understanding) and media pre-select to streamline communication</cite>.
- Trace subsystem couplings: examine how production/distribution link observer/integration and observation systems, and how genres calibrate society’s self-observation and expectations. <cite id="e4b81f40-2">Audience participation in self-observation via films</cite> <cite id="e4b81f40-3">Dissemination and symbolic media extend observation and expectation</cite>.
- Attend to paradox and reflexivity: look for “fitting–not-fitting” aesthetic strategies in mise-en-scène/narrative that enact the arts system’s evaluative paradox, while noting limits of purely binary models for cinematic meaning-making. <cite id="34163fc7-2">Arts communication driven by “fitting–not-fitting,” but this needs further development</cite> <cite id="34163fc7-1">Tensions between communication about art and communication through art</cite>.

Limits and future directions
- The framework is strongest on macro-structural couplings and communicative selection; it benefits from integration with theories that foreground ambiguity, materiality, and embodied experience—areas Luhmann explicitly flagged as gaps in culture and art. <cite id="34163fc7-1">Gaps in defining culture-as-process, undertheorized ambiguity, and focus on communication about rather than through art</cite> <cite id="34163fc7-2">Luhmann’s world is “not very physical” or “immediate,” underscoring the need to incorporate embodiment and immediacy</cite> <cite id="34163fc7-4">Risk of “black box” subsystems and arbitrariness in media-coding</cite>.

In the 1960s, Luhmann was influenced by Parsons' attempt to establish a universal sociological theory ("a theory for all cases") on the new system basis. However, later he changed his views: while in Parsons' theory the fundamental question was the preservation of structures and integration of the system, for Luhmann the key aspect was functional differentiation. Luhmann rejected Parsons' AGIL scheme and left aside Weber-Parsons' problem of individual action for he believed in the existence of a larger number of partial social systems than in Parsons' theory (but did not provide a comprehensive list of these partial systems). The fundamental way in which Parsons influenced Luhmann was showing him how to apply the system approach in sociology, and Luhmann was also influences by Parsons' later concept of the generalized media that he developed into a universal explanatory model. 

However, in his theoretical works, Luhmann used other sources of inspiration as well. The general framework of his reflections is the concept of self-organization based on the study of thermodynamic processes and dissipative structures of Ilya Prigogine. Luhmann also studied the general theory of systems founded by Ludwig von Bertalanffy [8], in which system is a complex of interacting elements; cybernetics (control of self-regulating systems) founded by Norbert Wiener [44]; and the "discourse of radical constructivism" [26] as an interdisciplinary study of cognitive processes, self-reference, organizational closeness and self-organization, which brought together researchers from the fields of cybernetics, biology, neurophysiology, psychology, psychiatry, philosophy, sociology and others.

Title: Risk or Totem?: Semantics of Child in Korean Risk Society
Snippet: In this article, several concepts proposed by Luhmann are employed to put forward the following hypothetic arguments: 1) the films of child abduction are to be considered as a certain form of self-observation of a risk society,3 and 2) the child represented in those films is an indicator of a specific "semantics" of child constituted under the dominant logic of a risk society. I will try to elucidate the following three key concepts employed in my hypothetic arguments: self-observation, meaning, and semantics. 

Firstly, "observation" in the Luhmannian systems theory is a technical notion defined as "any operation that makes a distinction, " or more expressly, "designation by distinction" (Luhmann 1984, p. 73). For Luhmann, it is always a system that observes itself or its environment rather than a human subject or consciousness. Observation is one of the many operations permitting the systems to conduct their self-referential and autopoietic reproductions. According to Luhmann, modern society, which is highly complex and functionally differentiated, observes itself through various forms, such as the sciences, mass media (news, advertisements, and entertainments), novels, films, works of art, etc. In particular, Luhmann enumerates two functional sub-systems, science and mass media, as the principal systems whose essential task consists of self-observation of society (Luhmann 1996(Luhmann , 1997(Luhmann , p. 1139)). He says that "what we know about our society, about the world in which we live, know, we know through the mass media" (Luhmann 1996, p. 9). Accordingly, when we attempt to examine the self-observation of a "risk society, " it would be worthwhile to refer to the films of child abduction (mass media) and discourses on risk society produced by various sociologists (science), given that both sociological discourses on risk society and films with a specific risk-related theme are a legitimate part of significant self-observations of a risk society.
</snippet>

Title: How to Define Media in a Mediatized Society? A Media Pedagogical Proposal Inspired by Theoretical Ideas of ­Castells, Luhmann and Peirce
Snippet: What is the specific benefit of reflecting media from a systems theory perspective? Niklas Luhmann's (1984;1988) systems theory perspective draws attention to a special way of modeling communication, which is different from our everyday life understanding of communication, e. g. face-to-face communication be tween people. This perspective allows us to analyze and to explain communi cation in technically supported networks in mass communication. Luhmann (1984) observes and describes, in terms of his approach, communication processes from a macro perspective. His system-related perspective shows that communication within a system follows certain rules. A basic assumption observes society as a social system, consisting not of individuals (subjects), but of communication. Correspondingly in these communications, individuals are not involved, but systems, to be more precise psychic systems. Following that, communication does not take place between people, but between communications (31). For Luhmann, communication is a process of three selections or rather a synthesis of three selections (ibid., 195 ff.). Understanding is the ability to differentiate between information and utterance. The first selection refers to information. This means that person A (a psychic system) decides to understand something as information. The second selection refers to the decision to transmit the information. This transmitted information can only be understood by a person -called B -if B can distinguish information and utterance, which means that B has to select again (third selection). This «understanding» is not a psychic understanding, but only refers to the selection. This means, that B does not necessarily have to act. It is a selection independent of the understanding. These contingent selections regarding communication initially make it seem rather improbable for communication to take place. In his theoretical approach Luhmann reduces this improbability through media and distinguishes language, media of dissemination and symbolically generalized communication media (ibid., 220 ff.). Language's task is to make the understanding of communication more likely. It widens the scope of communication possibilities beyond mere perception and makes it possible to connect psychic and social systems. The media of dissemination shall remove restrictions of communication regarding time and space and, thereby increase the addressees' reachability. Examples of dissemination media are writing, printing and electronic broadcasting, which were developed on the basis of language.

Title: Niklas Luhmann’s system theory: A critical analysis
Snippet: Apparently, what the observer observes depends on the perspective taken, which also applies to the system that observes itself and also to the researcher undertaking observations of the second degree. It is for this reason (though not only this reason) that sociology is a multiparadigmatic science, and that researchers observe social reality differently than Luhmann did (for this reason, Luhmann said little about his own observational position). 

Another important topic of discussions is the level of specificity of individual subsystems in Luhmann's theory. Perhaps, this is mainly the result of the 'methodological antihumanism' that, despite having written hundreds of articles on systems, Luhmann's works do not provide a detailed analysis of how the internal processes of systems operate. His approach identifies certain dominant characteristics of individual systems but goes into little detail. Everything is explained on the principle of symbolically generalized communication media, while systems remain mythical cybernetic 'black boxes'. 

The system theory (since Bertalanffy) tried to uncover some kind of universal key, a supermethodology tp explain individual processes in various types of systems. For Luhmann this universal key was the concept of generalized communication media introduced in sociology by Parsons. While Parsons, through the AGIL scheme, distinguished four types of such media -money, power, influence and value commitmentas corresponding to the bases of individual subsystems, Luhmann rejected this insisting that a much greater number of subsytems had their own ways of communication. The second feature of Luhmann's thought is the belief that these communication media, despite operating in different ways, are always binary coded -with positive and negative variants (how these communication media and their code originated is not clear). Luhmann's descriptions of communication media and codes often cause a feeling of arbitrariness. In general, Luhmann's interpretation of the functioning of individual subsystems is derived in a deductive manner from one pattern: the functioning of money in the economic system. This interpretation is based on a kind of faith in the single mechanism for the operation of all systems. 

Luhmann's concept of communication mainly ignores the material world with its phenomena and structures. From the philosophical perspective, this is a kind of idealism with no room for the material.

Title: Images of Thought and Acts of Creation: Deleuze, Bergson, and the Question of Cinema
Snippet: Images of Thought and Acts of Creation: Deleuze, Bergson, and the Question of Cinema 3 the temporal nature of film. The result is a fundamental destabilization of the very idea of a representation, displacing notions of signification and association in favor of acts of creation and images of thought. 

The greatest achievement of the Cinema books is that they suggest a means of looking at film that explodes static views of the work that the work of art does. Rather than "representing" something, film, for Deleuze, has the potential to create its own fluid movements and temporalities. These movements, while related to formal elements of rhythm and duration within the film itself, cannot be reduced to specific techniques or concrete images. Similarly, the temporality that Deleuze locates within the cinema cannot be pinned to a specific type of shot, nor a particular moment in the shooting, editing, projection, or reception of a film. By refusing to thus situate his theory, Deleuze completely sidesteps psychoanalytic and semiological film theories that would locate the "meaning" of film beneath the surface level of signs. The ramifications of Deleuze's project far exceed the scope of this paper. My goal, nevertheless, is to map several of its threads. The first is an interrogation of what varied meanings the term "representation" might have for Bergson or Deleuze with specific reference to cinema. 

The second involves the relationship between film and the realm that can be designated as the "real." Finally, the overarching question that motivates me is whether it is possible to maintain a commitment to the "art of living" that Bergson (and Deleuze) so convincingly promote while doing work on the "objects" of visual culture. 

These are lines of inquiry that I cannot exhaust, but at the same time, they are a movement toward understanding the creative potentials of thinking through and with the work of art. 

The Cinema books map a rift in filmmaking which can be roughly situated at the end of World War II. This split, however, cannot be reduced to a historical shift, but exists instead in differing configurations of movement and time. The movement-image, according to Deleuze, is exemplified by classical Hollywood cinema.

Title: The Autopoietic Character of Society
Snippet: In this chapter, we concentrate on the basic tenets of Niklas Luhmann's contribution who launched a very detailed description of society as an autopoietic system. Moving beyond the living physical systems, Luhmann abstracts the idea of 're-creation' into the nonphysical production of events and sees society as being re-created via communication. So when Luhmann "began to use autopoiesis in his work, Luhmann's approach was not crudely to apply autopoiesis to social systems but rather first of all to abstract the concept of autopoiesis away from the biological realm and then to apply this abstracted concept to social systems" ( [9], p.197). While Maturana did express his concerns about the transferability of autopoiesis in the social domain, it was actually Maturana himself that introduced Luhmann to autopoiesis, with Luhmann making it his life's work to describe social systems as autopoietic systems. The tension between these two different schools of thought on whether social systems can be rendered through autopoiesis has led to some very lively debates. Without a doubt, Luhmann's theory is elaborate so this chapter must restrict itself to the fundamental context and a few of the cardinal constructs that Luhmann deploys in the context of social autopoiesis. But before doing so, it is worth recognising that Luhmann is considered to be a pioneer in both systems theory and social theory ([10], p.1). Luhmann places central emphasis on the role of communication ([10], p.14) and builds his theory on the rich background of systems theory as "language for dealing with phenomena of recursiveness and co-evolution" ( [11], p.106) is necessary to describe social autopoiesis. 

In seeing his scholarly vision through, Luhmann built on the tradition of systems theory and second-order cybernetics in particular.

Below is a synthesis of how Niklas Luhmann’s systems theory describes cinema, grounded in his general theory of communication, differentiation, and autopoiesis, and in applications to art, media, and film.

Core concepts Luhmann brings to cinema
- Communication as structuration. In Luhmann’s view, society is composed of communication processes, not individuals acting on a common world; communication is a recursive “synthesis of three selections” (utterance, information, understanding) and occurs between communications, with psychic systems providing observation, expectation, and memory that feed and are fed by social systems. <cite id="e4b81f40-0">Communication is a three-fold selection: selection of utterance, selection of information, selection of understanding, and media arise as macro-structures to pre-select and streamline communication</cite> <cite id="e4b81f40-0">Observation, expectation and remembering are key; communications exist in time and must be tried again, so society builds “media” to facilitate remembering and pre-selection</cite> <cite id="e4b81f40-1">Communication processes are symbolically generalized couplings; Luhmann’s late work emphasizes observation and meta-observation as foundational, with media as symbolically generalized communication media</cite> <cite id="e4b81f40-3">Media of dissemination (writing, printing, broadcasting) remove time-space restrictions; language, dissemination media, and symbolically generalized communication media widen possibilities and connect psychic and social systems</cite>.
- Functional differentiation and subsystems. Modern society differentiates into autopoietic subsystems (e.g., politics, economy, science, art, law, religion, sport, health, education, mass media) whose operations are closed to each other and organized around binary distinctions; cinema belongs to the symbolic-media arts subsystems that select, store, and communicate cultural meaning. <cite id="e4b81f40-0">Ten systems can be enumerated and are autopoietic, operationally closed, with specific binary codes</cite> <cite id="e4b81f40-3">Language, dissemination media, and symbolically generalized media regulate communication possibilities and connect psychic and social systems</cite> <cite id="e4b81f40-2">Modern society observes itself through sciences and mass media; films, novels, and art participate in society’s self-observation</cite>.
- Autopoiesis and cultural production. Autopoietic systems reproduce themselves by producing and processing their own distinctions; in culture/arts, this means works and meanings are co-constituted in communicative couplings that are both self-referential and historically produced. <cite id="e4b81f40-2">Observation is one of the operations permitting systems to conduct self-referential and autopoietic reproductions; films and novels are legitimate parts of significant self-observations of society</cite> <cite id="e4b81f40-4">Luhmann’s approach identifies dominant characteristics of systems via symbolically generalized media; subsystems are “black boxes” with binary-coded communications</cite>.

Cinema as a communication system and medium of self-observation
- Cinema within mass media and culture. Luhmann treats mass media (news, advertisements, entertainments) as functional systems that communicate pre-selected differences to society; films are communicative artifacts produced within the arts system and circulate as media that present symbolized realities to society. <cite id="e4b81f40-0">Grand structures and “media” continuously arise to facilitate effective communication and remembering, pre-selecting and streamlining communication in society</cite> <cite id="e4b81f40-2">Modern society observes itself through mass media; what we know about our society we know through the mass media, which include films and entertainments</cite> <cite id="e4b81f40-3">Dissemination media expand reach across time and space; examples include writing, printing, and electronic broadcasting</cite>.
- Self-observation and reflexivity. Cinema participates in society’s “self-observation”: audiences learn themselves, their risks, norms, and conflicts through films, which means cinema is not only a cultural product but also a meta-communication that reflects and conditions social perception. <cite id="e4b81f40-2">Modern society’s essential task consists of self-observation via science and mass media; films are a legitimate part of this self-observation</cite> <cite id="e4b81f40-2">In particular, films of child abduction are considered self-observation of a risk society; the child becomes an indicator of a specific semantics constituted by the risk society</cite> <cite id="e4b81f40-0">Media are built up by communications within a system and are not “seen” by the systems using them; they provide pre-sets and configurations (language, values, structures) for effective communication</cite>.

Production and reception as couplings between observer/integration and observation
- Selection, storage, and distribution. Film production and exhibition operate as couplings that select, encode, and store differences (narratives, images, motifs) that can later be re-communicated; dissemination media (cinemas, broadcasting) make observation and expectation scalable across time and space. <cite id="e4b81f40-0">Media pre-select to streamline communication and remembering, making possible effective communication across time</cite> <cite id="e4b81f40-3">Dissemination media remove time-space restrictions and increase reach; they are built on language and broaden communication possibilities</cite>.
- Audiences as observers. Reception is not “meaning-making” by subjects but system-level selection: viewers distinguish utterance and information, align with selected codes, and thereby participate in reproducing the filmic system and its meanings. <cite id="e4b81f40-0">Understanding is the ability to differentiate between information and utterance; communication is a synthesis of three selections, independent of psychic understanding</cite> <cite id="e4b81f40-1">Observation is a technical notion as designation by distinction; systems (including psychic systems) observe themselves; the abstract notion of observation becomes central in Luhmann’s late work</cite> <cite id="e4b81f40-2">Accordingly, society knows itself through the mass media; films and art participate in this self-observation</cite>.

Autonomy, aesthetic paradox, and ambiguity in cinematic communication
- Art as a system of “fitting–not-fitting.” The arts system evaluates communicative artifacts by a functional paradox: works must simultaneously satisfy and violate criteria to count as art, a structure emphasized by Luhmann and critiqued as underdeveloped in theoretical terms. <cite id="34163fc7-1">Luhmann’s theory may frame cultural communication, but he provides limited theoretical development of the creative process in relation to culture and treats the arts as communication about art rather than through art</cite> <cite id="34163fc7-2">In Luhmann’s view, artworks communicate in a functional system driven by the paradoxical binary “fitting–not-fitting,” but this mode needs further theoretical development</cite>.
- Ambiguity and limits. Scholars note a tension between Luhmann’s binary coding and the ambiguous, open-ended character of aesthetic communication; cinema often relies on interpretive slippage that Luhmann’s strict dichotomies undertheorize. <cite id="34163fc7-1">Luhmann’s description of creation of the artwork mentions a “special kind of communication” but is not theoretically developed in relation to culture, and he describes the social system of the arts as communication about art rather than through art</cite> <cite id="34163fc7-2">Luhmann’s world is not very “physical” or “immediate,” and the paper theorizes “ambiguous communication” as central, contrasting with Luhmann’s binary “ambiguous–not-ambiguous” framing</cite> <cite id="34163fc7-2">Luhmann speaks of a “doubling” of meaning in mass media (constructing and making constructions realities) framed by “new information–old information,” creating a tension with a theory of “selection of ambiguity”</cite>.
- Media as “medium of media.” Cinema’s self-referential character is highlighted by its status in the mass media system as a medium that both explores possible realities and stabilizes them; filmic worlds exemplify the media’s role in constructing and validating social realities. <cite id="34163fc7-2">Mass-media construct reality or explore possible realities, e.g., in stories or sitcoms; “realities can be constructed and constructions can become realities”</cite> <cite id="e4b81f40-0">Media are built up over time by communications, invisible to the systems using them, and provide pre-sets and configurations for enduring and effective communications</cite>.

Cinema’s relation to other media and to society
- Coupling and differentiation. Cinema couples observer/integration systems (psychic systems) with observation systems (sensory, memory) via symbolically generalized media, extending language and dissemination technologies; it differs from language (symbolic generalization) and from broadcasting (distribution) in its integrated communicative form. <cite id="e4b81f40-3">Language, dissemination media, and symbolically generalized media operate as distinct layers; dissemination media expand reach, while language widens possibilities and connects psychic and social systems</cite>.
- Cultural communication and mass media. Within cultural communication, cinema is a specialized subsystem that communicates cultural pre-sets (values, norms, expectations) while also being evaluated by the arts system’s paradoxical criteria. <cite id="34163fc7-1">Cinema fits within cultural communication but Luhmann’s account undertheorizes the “special kind of communication” of art</cite> <cite id="34163fc7-2">The arts system is driven by “fitting–not-fitting,” while mass media construct and stabilize realities through stories, creating a tension that needs reflection</cite>.
- Societal totality and risk/society. Film genres and cycles can be read as society’s self-observation of specific problematics (e.g., risk) and as indicators of collective semantics and concerns. <cite id="e4b81f40-2">Films of child abduction are considered self-observation of a risk society; the child in those films indicates a semantics of child shaped by risk society</cite>.

Processual and developmental accounts
- Autopoietic production and reproduction. Films are produced as communicative structures that select and store differences, then reproduced in reception and distribution; over time, media pre-sets and cultural codes shift, altering what counts as meaningful filmic communication. <cite id="e4b81f40-0">Media are built up by communications within a system and remain “invisible” to the systems using them; they provide pre-sets that enable enduring and effective communication</cite> <cite id="e4b81f40-0">Communication must be “tried again,” so structures and media continuously arise to facilitate remembering and pre-selection</cite>.
- Historical differentiation and self-referentiality. Cinema emerges within modern society’s differentiation as a subsystem that both reflects and conditions social observation; as a “medium of media,” it recursively models and modulates how society sees itself. <cite id="e4b81f40-2">Sociology and mass media are principal systems of society’s self-observation; films, novels, and art participate in this self-observation</cite> <cite id="e4b81f40-3">Symbolically generalized media and dissemination media regulate communication across time and space, enabling modern media systems</cite>.

Critical perspectives and limits
- Ambiguity, embodiment, and immediacy. Luhmann’s framework has been criticized for undertheorizing ambiguity, emotions, and physical immediacy in art and communication, which are vital to cinematic experience and reception. <cite id="34163fc7-1">Luhmann leaves gaps with culture-as-process, and his account of creation of artworks is not theoretically developed; he emphasizes communication about art over communication through art</cite> <cite id="34163fc7-2">Luhmann’s world is “not very physical” or “immediate,” leaving little room for play, performativity, and cultural communication that requires embodiment and immediacy</cite>.
- Idealism vs. materiality and specificity. Critics argue Luhmann treats systems as “black boxes” and risks idealizing communication over material structures and media technologies, which hampers detailed analysis of filmic production and reception. <cite id="34163fc7-1">Luhmann’s description of the arts system as communication about art rather than through art is seen as insufficient</cite> <cite id="34163fc7-2">Luhmann’s “doubling” of meaning is framed by “new information–old information,” creating a tension with ambiguity</cite> <cite id="34163fc7-4">Luhmann’s approach identifies dominant characteristics via generalized media but offers little specificity; systems often remain mythical “black boxes” with possible arbitrariness in media-coding</cite> <cite id="34163fc7-4">Luhmann’s interpretation of communication media can seem idealistic with little room for the material world</cite>.

Putting it together: a Luhmannian description of cinema
- As a system: Cinema is an autopoietic subsystem of modern society that produces and reproduces its own distinctions through communicative artifacts; it is organized around binary codes (e.g., inside/outside, sense/reference, fitting/not-fitting) and is operationally closed from other subsystems. <cite id="e4b81f40-0">Systems are operationally closed and autopoietic; media arise to pre-select and streamline communication</cite> <cite id="34163fc7-2">Artworks communicate in a functional system driven by “fitting–not-fitting”</cite>.
- As communication: Film production and exhibition operate as couplings that select, encode, and distribute information; audiences receive as observers, differentiating utterance and information and thereby sustaining the filmic system. <cite id="e4b81f40-0">Communication is a three-fold selection; media pre-select to facilitate remembering and communication</cite> <cite id="e4b81f40-1">Observation is designation by distinction; late Luhmann centers observation and meta-observation</cite>.
- As self-observation: Cinema mediates society’s self-reflection—genres and cycles can be read as expressions and regulators of collective concerns (e.g., risk)—making film both mirror and mold social perception. <cite id="e4b81f40-2">Society knows itself through the mass media; films participate in this self-observation</cite> <cite id="e4b81f40-2">Films of child abduction exemplify self-observation of a risk society and index a risk-related semantics</cite>.
- As a medium of media: Cinema exemplifies the media’s power to construct and stabilize realities; narrative worlds and images become shared realities that can then be re-communicated across time and space. <cite id="34163fc7-2">Mass media construct and make constructions realities, e.g., through stories</cite> <cite id="e4b81f40-3">Dissemination media remove time-space constraints and expand reach, enabling modern communication systems</cite>.
- As art: Its aesthetic status depends on a paradoxical coupling—simultaneous adequacy and inadequacy to criteria—reflecting the arts system’s evaluative mode, even as Luhmann’s formalization struggles with ambiguity and embodiment. <cite id="34163fc7-2">Art communication is driven by the “fitting–not-fitting” paradox</cite> <cite id="34163fc7-1">Luhmann’s account is criticized for undertheorizing ambiguity and for focusing on communication about art rather than through art</cite>.

Practical implications for studying film
- Analyze film as communicative selection: focus on how scripts, editing, and sound select “differences” (events, rhythms, gaps) that are communicatively bound to audience codes. <cite id="e4b81f40-0">Communication requires the three selections (utterance, information, understanding) and media pre-select to streamline communication</cite>.
- Trace subsystem couplings: examine how production/distribution link observer/integration and observation systems, and how genres calibrate society’s self-observation and expectations. <cite id="e4b81f40-2">Audience participation in self-observation via films</cite> <cite id="e4b81f40-3">Dissemination and symbolic media extend observation and expectation</cite>.
- Attend to paradox and reflexivity: look for “fitting–not-fitting” aesthetic strategies in mise-en-scène/narrative that enact the arts system’s evaluative paradox, while noting limits of purely binary models for cinematic meaning-making. <cite id="34163fc7-2">Arts communication driven by “fitting–not-fitting,” but this needs further development</cite> <cite id="34163fc7-1">Tensions between communication about art and communication through art</cite>.

Limits and future directions
- The framework is strongest on macro-structural couplings and communicative selection; it benefits from integration with theories that foreground ambiguity, materiality, and embodied experience—areas Luhmann explicitly flagged as gaps in culture and art. <cite id="34163fc7-1">Gaps in defining culture-as-process, undertheorized ambiguity, and focus on communication about rather than through art</cite> <cite id="34163fc7-2">Luhmann’s world is “not very physical” or “immediate,” underscoring the need to incorporate embodiment and immediacy</cite> <cite id="34163fc7-4">Risk of “black box” subsystems and arbitrariness in media-coding</cite>.

Title: Towards a theory and practice of cultural communication
Snippet: Luhmann's social systems theory may be seen as an ultimate description of the systemic necessities of the process of communication. As such it may provide a strong and credible framework for a theory of cultural communication. There are however, as noted, some major issues to be addressed. The first is that Luhmann's theory does not provide any clear definition of culture-as-process: Luhmann seems strikingly hesitant on the subject of culture (Burkart and Runkel, 2004). The second is that his description of the process of creation of the art work (as communicative artefact) does mention "a special kind of communication" 21 in relation to the arts, but this "special kind of communication" is not theoretically developed in relation to culture. Thirdly, Luhmann seems to describe the social system of the arts in terms of communication about art and not primarily in terms of communication through (or with) art. Finally, although not mentioned above-but mentioned by others-the work of Luhmann leaves some gaps when it comes to embodiment and emotions as locus or driver of (inter)personal and societal processes, actions and experiences (Ciompi, 2004;Ciompi and Endert, 2011;Damasio, 2018). These issues may be addressed if the description of culture is more precisely taken apart, in particular in relation to ambiguous communication.

Title: Niklas Luhmann’s system theory: A critical analysis
Snippet: However, Luhmann as a theorist of social systems seems to be a 'realist. His typical claim -es gibt Systeme (there are systems) [23. P. 31] -expresses his idea that systems are not just thought-based constructions or scientific models but real things. In the 1960s, Luhmann was influenced by Parsons' attempt to establish a universal sociological theory ("a theory for all cases") on the new system basis. However, later he changed his views: while in Parsons' theory the fundamental question was the preservation of structures and integration of the system, for Luhmann the key aspect was functional differentiation. Luhmann rejected Parsons' AGIL scheme and left aside Weber-Parsons' problem of individual action for he believed in the existence of a larger number of partial social systems than in Parsons' theory (but did not provide a comprehensive list of these partial systems). The fundamental way in which Parsons influenced Luhmann was showing him how to apply the system approach in sociology, and Luhmann was also influences by Parsons' later concept of the generalized media that he developed into a universal explanatory model. 

However, in his theoretical works, Luhmann used other sources of inspiration as well. The general framework of his reflections is the concept of self-organization based on the study of thermodynamic processes and dissipative structures of Ilya Prigogine. Luhmann also studied the general theory of systems founded by Ludwig von Bertalanffy [8], in which system is a complex of interacting elements; cybernetics (control of self-regulating systems) founded by Norbert Wiener [44]; and the "discourse of radical constructivism" [26] as an interdisciplinary study of cognitive processes, self-reference, organizational closeness and self-organization, which brought together researchers from the fields of cybernetics, biology, neurophysiology, psychology, psychiatry, philosophy, sociology and others.

snippet.text: Luhmann's social systems theory may be seen as an ultimate description of the systemic necessities of the process of communication. As such it may provide a strong and credible framework for a theory of cultural communication. There are however, as noted, some major issues to be addressed. The first is that Luhmann's theory does not provide any clear definition of culture-as-process: Luhmann seems strikingly hesitant on the subject of culture (Burkart and Runkel, 2004). The second is that his description of the process of creation of the art work (as communicative artefact) does mention "a special kind of communication" 21 in relation to the arts, but this "special kind of communication" is not theoretically developed in relation to culture. Thirdly, Luhmann seems to describe the social system of the arts in terms of communication about art and not primarily in terms of communication through (or with) art. Finally, although not mentioned above-but mentioned by others-the work of Luhmann leaves some gaps when it comes to embodiment and emotions as locus or driver of (inter)personal and societal processes, actions and experiences (Ciompi, 2004;Ciompi and Endert, 2011;Damasio, 2018). These issues may be addressed if the description of culture is more precisely taken apart, in particular in relation to ambiguous communication.

However, Luhmann as a theorist of social systems seems to be a 'realist. His typical claim -es gibt Systeme (there are systems) [23. P. 31] -expresses his idea that systems are not just thought-based constructions or scientific models but real things. In the 1960s, Luhmann was influenced by Parsons' attempt to establish a universal sociological theory ("a theory for all cases") on the new system basis. However, later he changed his views: while in Parsons' theory the fundamental question was the preservation of structures and integration of the system, for Luhmann the key aspect was functional differentiation. Luhmann rejected Parsons' AGIL scheme and left aside Weber-Parsons' problem of individual action for he believed in the existence of a larger number of partial social systems than in Parsons' theory (but did not provide a comprehensive list of these partial systems). The fundamental way in which Parsons influenced Luhmann was showing him how to apply the system approach in sociology, and Luhmann was also influences by Parsons' later concept of the generalized media that he developed into a universal explanatory model. 

However, in his theoretical works, Luhmann used other sources of inspiration as well. The general framework of his reflections is the concept of self-organization based on the study of thermodynamic processes and dissipative structures of Ilya Prigogine. Luhmann also studied the general theory of systems founded by Ludwig von Bertalanffy [8], in which system is a complex of interacting elements; cybernetics (control of self-regulating systems) founded by Norbert Wiener [44]; and the "discourse of radical constructivism" [26] as an interdisciplinary study of cognitive processes, self-reference, organizational closeness and self-organization, which brought together researchers from the fields of cybernetics, biology, neurophysiology, psychology, psychiatry, philosophy, sociology and others.

Title: Risk or Totem?: Semantics of Child in Korean Risk Society
Snippet: In this article, several concepts proposed by Luhmann are employed to put forward the following hypothetic arguments: 1) the films of child abduction are to be considered as a certain form of self-observation of a risk society,3 and 2) the child represented in those films is an indicator of a specific "semantics" of child constituted under the dominant logic of a risk society. I will try to elucidate the following three key concepts employed in my hypothetic arguments: self-observation, meaning, and semantics. 

Firstly, "observation" in the Luhmannian systems theory is a technical notion defined as "any operation that makes a distinction, " or more expressly, "designation by distinction" (Luhmann 1984, p. 73). For Luhmann, it is always a system that observes itself or its environment rather than a human subject or consciousness. Observation is one of the many operations permitting the systems to conduct their self-referential and autopoietic reproductions. According to Luhmann, modern society, which is highly complex and functionally differentiated, observes itself through various forms, such as the sciences, mass media (news, advertisements, and entertainments), novels, films, works of art, etc. In particular, Luhmann enumerates two functional sub-systems, science and mass media, as the principal systems whose essential task consists of self-observation of society (Luhmann 1996(Luhmann , 1997(Luhmann , p. 1139)). He says that "what we know about our society, about the world in which we live, know, we know through the mass media" (Luhmann 1996, p. 9). Accordingly, when we attempt to examine the self-observation of a "risk society, " it would be worthwhile to refer to the films of child abduction (mass media) and discourses on risk society produced by various sociologists (science), given that both sociological discourses on risk society and films with a specific risk-related theme are a legitimate part of significant self-observations of a risk society.

Snippet: What is the specific benefit of reflecting media from a systems theory perspective? Niklas Luhmann's (1984;1988) systems theory perspective draws attention to a special way of modeling communication, which is different from our everyday life understanding of communication, e. g. face-to-face communication be tween people. This perspective allows us to analyze and to explain communi cation in technically supported networks in mass communication. Luhmann (1984) observes and describes, in terms of his approach, communication processes from a macro perspective. His system-related perspective shows that communication within a system follows certain rules. A basic assumption observes society as a social system, consisting not of individuals (subjects), but of communication. Correspondingly in these communications, individuals are not involved, but systems, to be more precise psychic systems. Following that, communication does not take place between people, but between communications (31). For Luhmann, communication is a process of three selections or rather a synthesis of three selections (ibid., 195 ff.). Understanding is the ability to differentiate between information and utterance. The first selection refers to information. This means that person A (a psychic system) decides to understand something as information. The second selection refers to the decision to transmit the information. This transmitted information can only be understood by a person -called B -if B can distinguish information and utterance, which means that B has to select again (third selection). This «understanding» is not a psychic understanding, but only refers to the selection. This means, that B does not necessarily have to act. It is a selection independent of the understanding. These contingent selections regarding communication initially make it seem rather improbable for communication to take place. In his theoretical approach Luhmann reduces this improbability through media and distinguishes language, media of dissemination and symbolically generalized communication media (ibid., 220 ff.). Language's task is to make the understanding of communication more likely. It widens the scope of communication possibilities beyond mere perception and makes it possible to connect psychic and social systems. The media of dissemination shall remove restrictions of communication regarding time and space and, thereby increase the addressees' reachability. Examples of dissemination media are writing, printing and electronic broadcasting, which were developed on the basis of language.

Title: Niklas Luhmann’s system theory: A critical analysis
Snippet: Apparently, what the observer observes depends on the perspective taken, which also applies to the system that observes itself and also to the researcher undertaking observations of the second degree. It is for this reason (though not only this reason) that sociology is a multiparadigmatic science, and that researchers observe social reality differently than Luhmann did (for this reason, Luhmann said little about his own observational position). 

Another important topic of discussions is the level of specificity of individual subsystems in Luhmann's theory. Perhaps, this is mainly the result of the 'methodological antihumanism' that, despite having written hundreds of articles on systems, Luhmann's works do not provide a detailed analysis of how the internal processes of systems operate. His approach identifies certain dominant characteristics of individual systems but goes into little detail. Everything is explained on the principle of symbolically generalized communication media, while systems remain mythical cybernetic 'black boxes'. 

The system theory (since Bertalanffy) tried to uncover some kind of universal key, a supermethodology tp explain individual processes in various types of systems. For Luhmann this universal key was the concept of generalized communication media introduced in sociology by Parsons. While Parsons, through the AGIL scheme, distinguished four types of such media -money, power, influence and value commitmentas corresponding to the bases of individual subsystems, Luhmann rejected this insisting that a much greater number of subsytems had their own ways of communication. The second feature of Luhmann's thought is the belief that these communication media, despite operating in different ways, are always binary coded -with positive and negative variants (how these communication media and their code originated is not clear). Luhmann's descriptions of communication media and codes often cause a feeling of arbitrariness. In general, Luhmann's interpretation of the functioning of individual subsystems is derived in a deductive manner from one pattern: the functioning of money in the economic system. This interpretation is based on a kind of faith in the single mechanism for the operation of all systems. 

Luhmann's concept of communication mainly ignores the material world with its phenomena and structures. From the philosophical perspective, this is a kind of idealism with no room for the material.
